extracted.intended_audience: patent examiners and patent practitioners (applicants and attorneys)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on examining and prosecuting claim definiteness and claim interpretation under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) (pre-AIA 112 second paragraph), including examiner actions, applicant responses, interviews, and when to document claim interpretation in reasons for allowance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definiteness requirement under 35 U.S.C. 112(b)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims must be sufficiently definite to inform the public of the bounds of the protected invention, i.e., what subject matter is covered by the exclusive rights of the patent. During prosecution, claims are given their broadest reasonable interpretation consistent with the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The focus is whether the claim meets threshold requirements of clarity and precision so that a person of ordinary skill can ascertain the metes and bounds and avoid infringement. Citation examples: Halliburton, In re Buszard, In re Yamamoto, In re Zletz; see MPEP § 2173.02 and related sections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner's duties when making a prima facie indefiniteness rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: When rejecting a claim as prima facie indefinite under 35 U.S.C. 112(b), the examiner should provide enough information in the Office action to permit applicant to make a meaningful response.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiner should point out the specific term or phrase that is indefinite, explain in detail why it renders the metes and bounds unclear, and, whenever practicable, indicate how the indefiniteness may be resolved. See MPEP § 707.07(d). If applicant does not adequately respond, the examiner may make the rejection final (e.g., Packard).

rubrics_metrics.name: Examination focus: clarity and precision, not preference for wording
rubrics_metrics.description: The focus during examination for compliance with definiteness is whether the claim meets clarity and precision thresholds, not whether more suitable language or modes of expression are available.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners are encouraged to suggest claim language to improve clarity but should not insist on their own preferences if applicant-selected language satisfies statutory requirement. If more information is necessary, a requirement under 37 CFR 1.105 may be appropriate (see MPEP § 704.10).

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant remedies for alleged indefiniteness
rubrics_metrics.description: An applicant may resolve ambiguity by amending the claims or by providing a persuasive explanation on the record that a person of ordinary skill would not consider the claim language unclear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In some cases applicant may provide separate definitions (e.g., art-recognized dictionary) or submit evidence (e.g., declaration under 37 CFR 1.132) to show how the ordinarily-skilled artisan would understand the term. If examiner is persuaded, the examiner should indicate in the next Office communication that the previous rejection has been withdrawn and explain what prompted the change (make specific reference to applicant's remarks).

rubrics_metrics.name: Make record clear to limit prosecution history estoppel
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners should provide explicit reasoning for making or withdrawing any rejection related to 35 U.S.C. 112(b) so the prosecution history clearly reflects the rationale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A clear and complete prosecution file record is important because prosecution history estoppel requires that claims be interpreted in light of PTO proceedings. Cite Festo: narrowing amendments made to satisfy Patent Act requirements may give rise to estoppel; examiners should clarify the record to show purpose of amendments or withdrawals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide claim interpretation in reasons for allowance when the record is unclear (37 CFR 1.104(e))
rubrics_metrics.description: If the examiner believes the prosecution record does not make clear the reasons for allowing a claim, the examiner may set forth such reasoning in reasons for allowance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One purpose is to improve quality/reliability of issued patents by providing a complete file history for public and patentee evaluation and to help avoid or simplify subsequent litigation. When allowing a claim based on an interpretation not readily apparent from the record, set forth the claim interpretation in reasons for allowance. Ensure statements do not place unwarranted broad or narrow interpretations on the claims (see MPEP §1302.14).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use interviews to resolve indefiniteness before rejecting
rubrics_metrics.description: Interviews are an effective examination tool and are encouraged when they can further prosecution, shorten pendency, or benefit examiner/applicant; issues of claim interpretation and clarity may often be resolved via interview.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners may initiate interviews to discuss broadest reasonable interpretation, meaning of claim limitations, scope of preamble language, functional language, intended use language, means-plus-function limitations, etc. The substance of any interview must be made of record in the application (MPEP §713.04; 37 CFR 1.2). Examples of 35 U.S.C. 112 issues to record include why a term is/is not clear, whether it invokes 112(f) and identification of corresponding structure/material/acts, and any claim amendments discussed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification should provide correspondence and antecedent basis for claim terms (37 CFR 1.75(d)(1))
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification should ideally serve as a glossary so examiner and public can ascertain the meaning of claim terms; claim terms must find clear support or antecedent basis in the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If specification lacks needed support/antecedent basis, object to the specification under 37 CFR 1.75(d)(1) and require applicant to amend description (without introducing new matter) or amend the claim. See MPEP §§608.01(o) and 2181.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims inconsistent with the specification may be indefinite
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim, although clear on its face, may be indefinite when a conflict between claimed subject matter and the specification disclosure renders claim scope uncertain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court examples (Moore, Cohn, Hammack, Anderson) show that internal inconsistencies between claim language and specification definitions/examples can render claims indefinite. Examiner should consider whether specification teaches or defines terms in a way that contradicts claim meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inconsistencies among claims can render claims indefinite
rubrics_metrics.description: Inconsistencies in the meaning of terms or phrases between claims may make the scope of claims uncertain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a disputed phrase is unclear, a skilled artisan may look to other claims for clarification (Philips v. AWH). Example: Tvngo Ltd. v. LG Elecs. — dependent claims using a phrase in a way that contradicts the independent claim can create indefiniteness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Breadth of a claim is not the same as indefiniteness
rubrics_metrics.description: A broad claim is not indefinite merely because it encompasses wide subject matter, provided the scope is clearly defined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A genus claim covering multiple species is broad but not indefinite if the scope is clear. Undue breadth should be addressed under appropriate statutory provisions depending on reason: if claim is too broad because it does not set forth what inventor regards as invention, consider 35 U.S.C. 112(b); if unsupported or not enabled, consider 35 U.S.C. 112(a); if reads on prior art, consider 35 U.S.C. 102 or 103.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaning of every term should be apparent; balance clarity with limits of language
rubrics_metrics.description: The meaning of every term used in a claim should be apparent from the prior art or the specification and drawings at filing. New terms are permissible but the clarity/precision requirement must be balanced with language and science limitations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants need not confine to prior art terminology but must make clear and precise the terms used to define the invention so metes and bounds can be ascertained. When specification states intended meaning, examine using that meaning (In re Zletz). If language is as precise as subject matter permits and apprises skilled artisans of utilization and scope, statute demands no more (see Packard). Examiners should suggest alternatives if language is not as precise as subject matter permits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Terms used contrary to ordinary meaning must be clearly redefined in the written description
rubrics_metrics.description: A patentee may act as lexicographer and redefine terms contrary to ordinary meaning, but the written description must clearly redefine the term so that a reasonable competitor or skilled artisan is put on notice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When more than one meaning exists for a term, applicant must make clear which meaning is relied upon; until the meaning is clear, a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) is appropriate. It is appropriate to compare technical dictionaries to ascertain accepted meaning in the art (In re Barr).

rubrics_metrics.name: Relative terminology and terms of degree are not automatically indefinite
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of relative terminology (terms of degree) does not automatically render a claim indefinite; acceptability depends on whether one of ordinary skill would understand what is claimed in light of the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a term of degree is used, the examiner should determine whether the specification provides some standard for measuring that degree or whether a recognized standard in the art exists. Examples: Interval Licensing, Hearing Components, Enzo Biochem, Seattle Box. If specification lacks a standard, applicant may overcome rejection with evidence (e.g., 37 CFR 1.132 declaration). Claims are indefinite if scope cannot be understood when read in light of the specification even if a term of degree is used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reference to a variable object may render a claim indefinite
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim may be indefinite when a limitation is defined by reference to an object and the relationship between the limitation and the object is not sufficiently defined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If elements admit two or more plausible constructions and examiner cannot ascertain positional/relational meaning, the claim may be indefinite (Ex parte Miyazaki, Ex parte Brummer). By contrast, phrases like 'so dimensioned as to be insertable through the space between the doorframe of an automobile and one of the seats' have been held definite (Orthokinetics). Consider whether the relationship is as accurate as the subject matter permits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Approximations (e.g., 'about') must be interpreted in context
rubrics_metrics.description: In determining the range encompassed by terms of approximation such as 'about,' one must consider the context of the term as used in the specification and claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The meaning of 'about' and similar approximations depends on context and the disclosure; examiners should look to specification context, examples, figures, and recognized standards in the art to determine the range encompassed.
